claims.text: A Ni-based high-entropy-alloy coating can successfully adhere to a Cu matrix.
Ni tends to form favorable metallurgical bonds with Cu.
The multiprincipal-element nature of an HEA promotes interfacial intermetallic formation.
The multiprincipal-element nature of the coating promotes formation of a graded transition zone.
A graded transition zone minimizes thermal mismatch and improves wear resistance.
The initial material is an untreated conventional Cu substrate.
A Ni-rich HEA coating is applied to the Cu substrate by a process such as laser cladding.
Controlled thermal input and ambient-atmosphere deposition can promote interfacial diffusion and permit intermetallic-phase formation and a graded interface.
Ni and Cu interdiffuse at the coating-substrate interface.
Ni-Cu interdiffusion creates intermetallic compounds or a solid-solution layer forming a graded interfacial region.
Ni-Cu intermetallic or solid-solution phases enhance metallurgical bonding at the interface.
The graded interface mitigates thermal-expansion mismatch and inhibits rapid wear.
The Ni-based HEA coating will have improved adhesion on Cu because of enhanced interfacial bonding.
The coated Cu will have superior wear resistance relative to uncoated Cu.
Coating performance and interface formation depend on laser-cladding parameters and the exact HEA composition.
Failure to optimize processing conditions may compromise formation of the graded interface.

contradictions.description: The proposed mediator and mechanism allow either an intermetallic compound or a solid-solution layer to provide bonding, but the falsification rule treats absence of detectable intermetallic formation as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis, even if the allowed solid-solution pathway occurs.
